RevText: I have owned this drill for 2 years now and have had it break down twice. It has seen fairly little work since I bought a drill better up to the task (Bosch 11255VSR). I also own an old Black & Decker (model number unreadable but similar to the DR260B) drill that is used for most more common tasks (picture hanging, furniture repair and the occasional abuse like concrete mixing). The first time the DeWalt broke down (2nd usage) was when I tried to drill a hole (1/4") in a concrete slab in hammer mode. (It quickly became hot and then stopped working.) I sent it in for repair under warranty and got it back. The Bosch did this task without any problems (to be expected since its a way heavier duty drill). I might have used the DW511 4-5 times since when it was the first drill I found in the garage when I needed to mix some thinset for tiling and again exact same behavior as before - it got hot and burned out. Then switched to the B&D; which completed the task (and 4 more bags) without any complaints!Since it's out of warranty I took it apart to see what's wrong with it. Turns out the brush holders have melted, which caused the brushes to no longer make contact. Just because I like fixing things I ordered the spare parts ($15 + $10 shipping) from DeWalt but I doubt the drill will see much use. I think the B&D; will do most things and when there is concrete I will use the Bosch. It's a shame since in general I like my DeWalt tools but the DW511 has been nothing but trouble. Would absolutely not recommend, especially if you only need one drill.

This is a definite recommend for any LP 6gal Hot Water Heater, whether Suburban or Atwood. Cut my LP refills from once a week to every 2 weeks. Kit contains all hardware necessary as well as written instructions. Tools necessary are open end wrenches (or socket set or vise grips), Teflon tape, drill with 1/8" bit, and Phillips screwdriver.First, turn off propane to water heater (turn interior thermostat to OFF; this will never be turned ON/PILOT again unless you need an emergency shower as the electric heating requires much more time to heat). Open pressure relief valve on the outside and allow (HOT!) water to flush out of the Water Heater until the temperature of water is cool to touch then close the valve. Turn water pump OFF. Remove drain plug with socket, open end wrench, or vise grip (I do not recommend any other tool as they may round hex edges) and allow water heater to drain completely. Use a water heater rinsing tool at this point to flush out interior of calcium build-up. It is also wise to screw on a bottle of white vinegar onto the rinsing tool, add it into the water heater, lightly screw the drain plug back on to allow the vinegar to eat any remaining calcium or build-up, and then flush out again after sitting 10 minutes or so.Wrap the threads of the anode and anode adapter with Teflon tape. Screw in the adapter (large for Suburban, small for Atwood) hand tight and then tighten slightly with open end wrench (not too tight since rinsing out water heater is a routine maintenance procedure every 6 months). Screw anode into center of adapter hand tight and then tighten slightly with open end wrench (definitely do NOT over tighten as may damage anode).Thread provided electric cable through vent of water heater so at least 1 foot of cord is inside water heater. Drill an 1/8" hole into the inside of the water heater, preferably above the propane line that enters the inside of the RV cabin. Place the provided "loop" onto the cord, about 3" behind the prong end. Separate the 3 prongs of the cord and place the ring prong over the drilled hole. Insert provided screw through the "loop" and screw it into the drilled hole.Balance the provided thermostat to the flattest side of pressure relief valve that allows the thermostat controls to be accessible. The default temperature is adequate to start and can be adjusted to a higher temperature at a later time (take temperature of water as it comes out of the faucet with thermometer and adjust thermostat until desired temperature reached). Secure the thermostat with the provided zip ties.Now match all colored prongs to one another and connect. Then turn back on your water pump so the water heater can refill. Once the water pump is silent, open the pressure relief valve temporarily just to release any air trapped within the water heater. Also, at this point if any water is visibly dripping from the anode/adapter drain assembly, tighten as needed with open wrench. Finally, ONLY after heater is full, plug the electric cable into an outlet and let the hot water heat (anode not submerged in water may become damaged). An additional outlet may be available at the back of the fridge, but I preferred a large gauge extension cord that I plugged into shore power to prevent blowing a breaker and allowed the cable end to tuck under the RV to stay out of the weather.

There are all sorts of grades of furnace filters--this one is a picks up an amazing amount of dirt. I'm always astonished when I go to change the filter. We live in an agricultural area so when the corn and soybeans are harvested, there is a lot of dust blowing around. And during summer, it's frequently a drought and again, it's dusty. This filter picks up the dust, and even seems to find the soot that drifts up from the coal-fired power plant south of here about fifty miles.  I keep a box of these in the basement, next to the furnace. In some months, I have to change them frequently. It makes a difference in the air quality in the house.The 1500 MPR (micro particle rating) is said to pick up dust, pet dander, mold, dust mite effluvia and even smoke and smog. I do notice a big difference--and my dog has allergies and if I need to change the filter, I know because she starts to sneeze.One trick I learned from a friend--if you buy your filters at your local home supply store, store your filter size on a note on your cell phone. You'll have it ready whenever you need to restock.

RevText: This is an interesting tool belt.  My philosophy is that one side is for nails and fasteners, plus punches and a nail puller, maybe a chisel--things that you'll use with your non-dominant hand (in my case the right).  The other side will have your hammer, a place for your battery drill, snips or pliers, writing utensils, and utility knife--things that you'll use with your dominant hand (my left).  This belt had a lot of pockets, but they seemed somewhat randomly placed.  Even for a right hander, there isn't a really good place for multiple pencils and a knife.  There are so many pockets, there's probably some place to put any tool, but it may not be very efficient.It does have big pockets.  Any battery drill should fit.  The belt is kind of cheap.  The holes are just punched into the leather and not reinforced.  The belt will probably wear out before the pouches.If you want to carry a lot of tools, this will hold them.  If you like to travel light and efficient, this might not be for you.

RevText: After buying "TTi Charge" as a gift for my dad, I decided to buy myself a more humble "New Wave" based on the idea that this is almost the same tool just without S30V for the blade and with a steel frame instead of a titanium one. Also, here there are no additional bit-driver inserts, no detachable clip and lanyard ring, the sheath is slightly cheaper... Actually, the perfect set: only things I really will use. The idea of saving did not included lower expectations on quality; after all, "made in USA", and Leatherman, and this model supposed to be not "el cheapo"... you got the idea. Well, the idea was wrong.Now I have both tools in my hands. Yes, they are almost identical in terms of tool-set and general design except for the cutting hook on serrated blade and slightly different shape of pliers head on TTi Charge. That's fine. What is different, is quality. The TTi Charge is a dream: smooth one-hand opening of the blades, easy opening and closing of all the tools, perfect finishing. The "New Wave" I received is just the opposite: finishing of the frame and of the primary blade is poor, assembly quality is so bad that it is impossible to open either blade one-handed and sometimes even with both hands, some of the small tools is very difficult to put back, pliers are very tight and open with a creaky sound.Some people complained about this product not made in the US. I think it's because of the small sticker inside of the box that says something like "part xxx made in China." I don't remember this number now, but I found that this is the sheath number. I don't care about sheath, probably would not use it anyway. Everything else matches the description: set of the tools, photo etc. Seller was "Amazon, LLC." Comparing two tools, "TTi Charge" and "New Wave", side by side made me think that this "New Wave" is authentic: most of the small tools looks identical with those in "TTi Charge". Just the overall quality of the "New Wave" is worse, much worse.I am disappointed; yes the price is lower than of TTi Charge, but it is still not a cheap product, and extra price in TTi includes such pricy things as S30V blade and titanium frame, and also numerous additional parts. How it explains such difference in the quality?I will not comment on performance of this tool, since I did not start to use it, and will not even try my luck with it, because with such poor assembly quality it is not convenient tool to use. Will send it back for a refund.

I have other Dewalt tools that I like (a power miter, for example) but this saber saw is a piece of junk.  But first, the positives:- It has very good power.- Vibration is minimal.- Easy to change bladesNow to the negatives, which (to me) would keep me from ever buying another Dewalt saber saw.-  If cutting through anything "challenging" like 3/4 plywood or oak, the blade will wander out of the guides with the least provocation.  With this saw, I have had to limit myself to cutting thin plywood (1/4" lauan, for example) or soft pine 3/4" or thinner, if I have to make any curved cuts.  Loses at least 20% of usability with that problem.- The saw comes with a place for a rip fence, but (1) no rip fence is included, and (2) no screw to secure an aftermarket rip fence is included.  This drops another 20% of usability, right there.-  Worst part: the pivoting shoe.  The shoe has a "lock" but the lock is worthless.  It wanders out of place, even when the shoe is slipped into the supposed "locking" position of 90-degrees.  If you push the shoe forward to enable pivoting to anything other than 90-degrees, the shoe will NOT LOCK INTO PLACE.  It is loose and slips constantly.I approached the tool guru at the local home store (it can't be named here) and asked him about this, since he worked for Dewalt at one time.  He just sighed and said that "Yes, it is a known problem."  He recommended that I wrap some 12-gauge wire around the body of the saw, to hold the locking lever in place (!?!?!)  I tried it, but even doing that does not lock the shoe into any bevel position--only at the 90-degree position.To me, this last issue makes the tool only about 25% usable.  I can use it to zip off a short piece of PVC pipe, or knock off a bit of offending wood from the end of a longer cut, but other than that it is worthless to me.  Either of those I could do with a $20 dollar handsaw.DON'T WASTE YOUR MONEY ON THIS SAW!

RevText: My more than 20 year old Sears pump began leaking and was not economical to repair when compared to the cost of a new pump. After reading the other reviews of this pump and checking out the price, it seemed to be a comparable replacement. There are many things to like about it and only a few to dislike.Our application is on a pressure tank to boost municipal water pressure, not a well...so your mileage may vary.I read many comments regarding the quiet and fast operation of this pump...I can say I don't agree with either. It's a little noisier than my old cast metal pump - the plastic has a harsh loudness to it and doesn't seem to dampen the noise as well as the old one. And it's neither slower or faster than the old pump.So, if you are replacing a similar 1/2 HP, 120V pump, don't expect miracles from this one.I liked the price, it's lighter than the metal pump and it's physical size was close enough to the old one that I did not have to make substantial changes to the plumbing. That's a big plus.The biggest negative in my mind centers on the plastic pump. It's noisy and the pump arrives with an over-tightening warning label stuck to it. Plastic housing made me uneasy and it was difficult to get the fittings tight enough to stop several small annoying leaks. Just be careful and eventually you'll get it. Determining how tight is "too tight" is always a guess so start too loose and work it in from there.Overall, I don't expect this pump to work for more than 20 years like the old one did...and I find it tiresome that we are continually forced as consumers to take "almost as good" in a tradeoff for lower prices and overall cheaper and slightly "less good" merchandise. I'd pay more to buy the exact same pump I replaced, but it's not available any more.This isn't a bad pump, it's just not as good as you could get in the past.
RevTitle: Typical modern product...good but not as good as the one it replaced

I ordered this optional blower with a ProCom plaque heater.  My mechanical-engineering experience told me not to expect much from the use of this blower.  The blower takes some of the radiant heat, which heats objects in the room, and converts it to convection heating of the room air.  Since the fan cools the plaques, you should expect to get less radiant heat when the fan is operating.  There might be no difference in the room heating, whether the fan runs or not.  But operation of the fan requires a small amount of electrical work, which becomes additional room heat.  This is a very small effect, possibly undetectable.  The automatic control of the fan, allows the fan to run only when the plaque heaters are hot.  When the plaque-heaters are not hot, the fan does not blow any cold air.  This is a nice feature, and works very well.So far, my experience with this fan shows that my initial expectations seem to be correct.  Possibly the only effect of the fan may be psychological.  If you hear the fan operating, you feel that something must be happening.  But so far I have not been able to detect any heating difference with the fan on or off.  If ProCom has collected any data showing different results, I would be happy to see the data.Bottom line, the fan is well constructed, installs easily, and has a nice automatic feature.  But it may be nothing more than a placebo, as far as heating your room.

As others mentioned, this stand suffers from material and workmanship deficiencies.  The steel components are poorly formed in places and holes do not always line up, requiring some creative assembly techniques.  The top is somewhat as described, a "butcher block finish" consisting of low density pressed paper covered with contact paper - I wouldn't even call it MDF.That said, I am not completely unhappy with the purchase since it was quite inexpensive. I would not be happy if I had paid more.  I would not recommend this to someone with limited experience in making things work.I am using it with a heavy Rikon 6x48"/10" belt/disc sander and so far it is sturdy, without wobble or shake after a few weeks of sanding.  I don't think I would use it with casters without adding extra reinforcement, for example a stiffening plywood shelf.  Also, my sander had a big enough footprint that I was able to fasten some bolts through the upper steel brackets which probably helped.  The safest thing for general use may be to toss the paper top and make one from plywood.Some tips.  When assembling the frame the bolt holes are difficult to line up in places, especially on the upper brackets.  This is far easier with a drift pin, standard industry practice.  I used a sturdy awl I had ground from an old screwdriver to force the holes onto alignment.  I've used this on plenty of other assemblies including things I've built from scratch.  Make sure ALL the bolts are kept loose until the end after setting the stand upright on a level surface.  I tighten all moderately then retighten.  The included bolts seem undersized to me and low quality so don't over-tighten.When drilling holes for the top be careful of the bit selection.  This is important when putting screws into any pressed fiber board products and especially with this low quality top.  If the drill bit is too big the screws will easily strip and not hold - if the bit is too small the pressboard will probably split.  The bit size should closely match the screw shaft not including the threads.  One trick with crumbly materials is to squirt a bit of wood glue into the hole before tightening he screw.  In any case, don't over-tighten!Since the steel is not a very heavy gauge, stiffening the entire stand with a plywood shelf might be a good thing if used with a planer or some tool stressed with heavy boards or having significant vibration.  Also, a heavy tool with a narrow footprint might benefit from adding some reinforcement to pressboard top in the short dimension since the maker failed to (or simply make a sturdy plywood top)Overall I'm satisfied with the stand and might even buy another one if the price is ever reduced to make up for the extra assembly effort and possible modifications needed. It is certainly functional for my application and less effort than cutting angle iron and making a sturdier stand from scratch, although assembly by welding would be far quicker than with all those screws.

RevText: I have used this Kreg fixture bar on my table saw cross cut sleds for 2 years.  I'm now ordering another for a box cutting jig on my band saw. I am a jig building fanatic.  This Kreg bar allowed me to build the most accurate cross cut sled I have made in 30 years.  For years, and many jigs I would try to dial in wood slot runners with tedious work and questionable function.  I would kill myself trying to get a wood runner sled to work with no slop and end up with 1/32 to 1/16 slop from the wood runner moving in the slot through the length of cut. These Kreg bars allow you to not only dial in the accuracy with the nylon adjusters with zero play, but to do it with as little, or as much friction in the sliding as you want. Amazing, a revelation to me.  I should add that I build adjustment into the fence on my sleds for use if  needed.  When I assembled the cross cut sled with the Kreg bar I lucked out, I got the bars square and didn't need to adjust the fence.  The Reviewers who had trouble keeping the bar aligned while screwing in place should note-I've been there too.  To get it right the easy way, first get a full length line drawn perfectly square on the jig bottom where the Kreg bar will go.  Set the bar exactly to the side of the line so you can still see it.  Here's the good part, clamp that sucker down at both ends so it can't move.  This is why God gave woodworkers clamps.  Then use a self centering drill bit in the bars countersunk holes.  Screw the bar down, remove the clamps and be tickled that it is exactly where you wanted it. Take your time to dial it in with the adjusters so there is no play in the slot and sliding friction  is as you wish. You will find the slightest turn of the adjuster makes a change in play and friction.  Take your time here.  If you get is where you like it and the cut isn't square, use your jig's fence adjustment.

When my house was built, I never even considered selecting ceiling fans.  I allowed the contractor to install whatever was included in the home package.  If I could go back in time, I would make sure this model was never even an option.  It is too loud and takes too much time to clear the moisture in a small bathroom after a shower.  It works and I have never had any mold issues but I have to run it about 45 minutes just to clear the condensation off the mirrors.  Another half hour so that the room is not "muggy".I thought I would at least warn other potential buyers.  I can think of better things to do than spend several hours navigating an attic filled with blown in insulation, searching for the fan, removing it, cutting a larger drywall opening, mounting and rewiring the replacement, routing the duct, and then cleaning up all the insulation that I tracked into the house. It is the task that I have to endure as punishment for not thinking ahead. If you are already planning on having to do that much work, get a better unit so you will have something to show for all your effort.I can understand wanting to find a replacement that is the same size as your existing model but if you are going to replace your fan, do it right the first time.  If it is a new installation, then don't even waste your time with this model.  Even if it was rated at twice the CFM, you wouldn't experience that kind of airflow for long because the openings on the grille are very small and plug up with lint fairly quickly.Just to give you some perspective, a single PC case fan in many computers moves more air than this model and doesn't make a racket in the process.  Several are typically used to move air through a space normally less than 4 cubic feet.  The CFM on this ceiling fan is lower and yet it is responsible for clearing the moisture out of a room that is ~200 cubic feet or larger.  This unit would be more suitable for a Honey Bucket.I am typically a sucker for products that are low priced.  Who doesn't love a great deal?  The price on this model is really low and if you want to look at cost/years of service, then this certainly is an excellent value.  If you use the fan daily and care about performance, then don't cut corners.  Your ears and bathroom walls will be much better off.(I just read some other reviews after mine was posted.  Purchasing this item to use for replacement parts is a brilliant idea if you desire a quick repair of an existing unit.  After about 10 years of enduring substandard performance, I look forward to retiring this model permanently.)

RevText: OK, if you have a well think of it as a underground water system like a river and know your water quality is constantly changing from one season to the next. So, consider testing at least 2x a year. This test will check for the basics and keep it affordable.I have a deep well, a water softener, a whole house filter(by the water tank) which filters out a lot of black metallic crap, a reverse osmoses system for drinking water and a basic fridge filter that comes with the refrigerator. Even with all of this, I still had concerns with my drinking water. Maybe fear that the RO system is getting old (14years or more), fear of Bacteria from septic's leaching into my well or the fact that my water just didn't taste as good as it has through the years. Not smelly or terrible tasting...just not as good as before. Biggest concern was high concentrations of metals and bacteria which in long exposure could give you a long list of health issues and good luck having a doctor figure out what's causing any of the symptoms. This kit tested for bacteria, lead, pesticides, nitrate, pH, hardness, chlorine(um...why have chlorine test for a well test kit? maybe treated wells?) copper and Iron. All tested negative which is a good feeling...for now. Interestingly enough is, my water is too soft and has a low pH which can cause leaching of copper and lead from the pipes! Also, the "different flavor" in my drinking water is the fact it has a low pH which is acidic. Have to get my water softener serviced. I'm very glad the pesticide tested negative too...there's 250 acres of old farm land across from my well, used for hay now but who knows what they grew and sprayed there years ago.  Overall, this is a basic test that will raise some flags if there is an issue and you can spend the big bucks for extensive testing then. Remember that the water quality is always changing in your well and the dude charging you the big bucks will point that fact out as he's doing his test :)
RevTitle: Simple test for my well water...not the most extensive, but good enough

This is my 3rd Leatherman Wave.  The first one was a "found" gift from an airlines unclaimed lost-and-found bin (after the passenger realized they couldn't fly with it, of course).  It was one of the classic models with a few minor differences in the auxiliary tools.  Then I lost it at a job site.  Purchased a second, more modern one from a local sporting-good store.  Lost that one at a job site a couple years later, too.  Now I have this one in black (woo!).  The included MOLLE sheath is going to be attached to a new toolbag I'm buying for purposes of getting MOLLE mounts.  With luck I won't lose this one.Out of the box, both this model and the stainless-finished model from before were quite difficult to operate.  The hinges are quite stiff.  They do need a little time to break-in and can be helped along a little with some strategic lubrication - lightweight oil works great but don't use WD40 unless you plan to keep doing it periodically.  I usually just dunk the whole thing in, pull it out, work all the moving parts a few times, then thoroughly wipe off any excess.As for tools, it's great.  But I would say that, wouldn't I, having owned 3 of them now?  The knife stays sharp enough for long enough that I generally only need to have it sharpened about once per year.  The pliers aren't spring-loaded, but that's a feature, here.  I use the wire cutters often, but they're used to strip Cat5 cable strands prior to installation in a terminal block and, for that, they're excellent.I like the black finish but I have my doubts about the durability of the finish.  It probably would have been more durable with a full anodizing or, as some other reviewers suggested, a process used for gun parts.  But then I'm not sure how they'd have to adjust their final assembly process to account for the different finish.  Based on how easily it appears to rub off, it's probably deposited copper selenium compound.  Don't get me wrong - it's not going to affect performance of the tool since the Wave is made of stainless steel underneath, anyway.  But if your life depends on not being seen, it could be an issue.  I suppose you could have it re-coated at some point, as well, or just use a sharpie pen to fill the gaps and scratches.Seeing as how a matte black finish is a strong selling point to the military, the included sheath is a nylon MOLLE type typically found on military bags, vests, helmets, etc., rather than the traditional leather belt-friendly sheath.  I suppose you could wrap it around your belt, but it's kind of missing the point.  Mounted to a MOLLE pack, this sheath isn't going to go anywhere.

I purchased this Elenco SR3B Professional Soldering Iron because it was only $16 compared to $42 for a Weller WP25 soldering iron.  The Weller WP25 and Weller WP35 have their soldering tips held in place by a knurl nut at the tip of the soldering iron barrel near the soldering iron tip.  With repeated uses the knurl nut becomes oxidized and corroded and it can become near to impossible to remove it. With the Elenco SR3B the knurl nut is near the end of the handle away from the heating element and away from the soldering tip which means it is far less susceptible to the heating and cooling effects of the heating element. This iron's knurl nut will  become far less oxidized and corroded like the Weller and Ungar Soldering irons.Before I even plug in a new soldering iron for the first time, I always remove the knurl nut and put anti-seize compound on the knurl nut threads and re tighten the knurl nut.  I then also put flux on the solder iron tip before I even plug it in for the first time.  After I plug in the soldering iron, I immediately put solder on the tip and hold it there until it melts so the tip can NOT become oxidized.  When I finish soldering I unplug the iron wipe it on the sponge quickly and add more solder to the tip until the tip cools down to the point where it cannot melt the solder any more.  This prevents the tip from becoming oxidized as the tip is cooling down.The only CON I can find in this soldering iron is the big metal ring that is secured into the handle by three screws.  This ring gets hot and can burn your finger if you touch it.  As long as you keep your fingers on the yellow rubber sleeve you won't have any problems.  The Weller SL325, SL335 and SL345 also have this metal socket which holds the heater in near the handle which can burn your finger.  The Weller WP25, WP35 and WP45 have a plastic ring which holds the heater in which stays cool to the touch.
RevTitle: Excellent iron, great tip that doesn't oxidize, nice 6' 3 prong plug.  Metal Ring held into handle by 3 screws gets very hot.

So a reading on a Bell meter that shows 9mG will show 100+mG on the Trifield.  This is due to feedback from computers, lights, and other machines into the (mostly) ground wiring.  We had some readings of 600hz in some areas.  The Trifield is good for the price BUT do not rely on it to tear your house apart to find a field issue.  We ended up purchasing a Bell 4100 series meter to confirm the repairs after the electricians fixed the problems.

Well its not too expensive and it really helps out by lining things up.  Two things to keep in mind however -1) If using on wooden doors, it will probably be fine but know that this part is plastic and plastic gives. Even after using screws to brace, when I used it on the metal door there was a fair amount of movement before the holesaw finally went in. Brace with your hand firmly to reduce the amount of movement.2) There really is a KEY illustration and instruction missing from the directions and that is the fact that you will need to remove the threaded nut that is on the mandrel for it to fit the smaller bore holesaw. What will happen is you will inevitably drill through the larger hole ready to swap out the holesaw bit and find that it does not fit. Don't panic. You have all the parts. Do this - Remove the small slotted screw holding the bit. Take a Phillips head screwdriver and put it in this hole. Take a pair of vice grips and YES, it will need to be vice grips for the torque you're going to need. Then, turn COUNTER CLOCKWISE to remove the threaded nut. (Some folks were saying its reverse thread and to turn clockwise - do NOT, you will only be tightening it more and making it worse). You may even be able to push the screwdriver and vice grips is opposite directions and get it to come off. One good frustrated push in this direction and it loosened it for me. You will then reveal the smaller set of threads which will go on the smaller holesaw bit. If doing again fresh out the package, I might even unsrew this bit first and drill the side hole and then move on to the larger 2 inch bit. Starting with the larger one only seems to tighten the thread onto the screws that much more.NOTE: I wouldn't even bother with the strike plate "guide" - it is absolutely worthless. Its made from plastic so is a horrible guide for a metal drill bit which, instead of being guided, could easily drill into the plastic piece-- which it did. Just use a chisel

The idea is to set it with the calibration screw to the Good mark when the filter is new.  Then when it starts plugging up, it works its way to the Red range.  That sounded like and excellent concept, and I don't know how anyone could do much better.  I didn't have the install problems others had.  I thought it went really well, and was quite pleased with the way it looked and worked when I was finished.  I believe for most people, the furnace is not a very big duck in their pond, until there is a problem.  They replace the filter when they think about it, which may or may not be when it actually needs it.  I was thinking this might help.Reasons it didn't work out.1.  Different medium have different restriction.  The furnace even say what to use, and what to expect from the different types, and the restriction build between clean and dirty is different.  Thus, I can't know if it is time to change the filter when the needle goes into the red.2.  My furnace is a 90%+ furnace as is common these days.  The blower runs at all different CFMs, based on what the controller decides based on its sensors, and whether you are running heat, AC, or just the circulation fan, and the CFM range is huge.  My furnace even says it auto-compensates for filter restrictions when it starts to get dirty.  However, the device can only be calibrated for one CFM.  It might work better on a furnace with a fixed speed blower and standard 1" thick fiberglass filter.3.  Will you actually look at it?  I didn't, once the novelty wore off.  I looked at it when there seemed to be not much air coming out, and then it was way overdue.I believe the furnace manufacturer is in the best position to tell you when the filter needs to be changed.  They are the ones that shut the furnace down when it gets too high.  They know the blower RPM and pressure differentials which means they could also indicate when things are getting out of hand.  At least give us an altitude chart, and where things need to be, and someone will make such a device with a little alarm that is adjustable for max. differential pressure, kind of like when a smoke detector battery is getting low.The closest thing we have today is the newer programmable thermostats keep track of the run hours, and shows a percent filter life remaining based on a swag that you entered as to how many average run hours you get out of a filter.  You look at the thermostat a lot more than the furnace, and MIGHT actually notice the bar graph and % filter life remaining.The needle fell of mine after years of use, but I'm not downgrading the rating at all for that.  My opinion is based on the above factors.  I'll just put a little black plastic press plug in the small hole where it currently is, and call it good.  If I believed it was telling me anything useful, I would give it 5 stars and buy another.

The best kind of product -- one that actually does what it claims to do! And it's a fraction of the cost of those adhesive films. Other commenters have done a great job describing the product, so I'm just going to give some tips.TO APPLY: You can find directions in these comments or elsewhere online. Make sure to buy (cheap) eye goggles and a nose/mouth mask to wear when applying, and to do so in a VERY ventilated area. I personally used 3 (quick) coats. Note that the end product does not come out 100% even...more like 90%. I like the slight unevenness, but if that will drive you crazy, go with the adhesive sheets.TO REMOVE: Use paper towels soaked in Rust-Oleum Lacquer Thinner and some elbow grease. Don't bother with nail polish remover, acetone or household cleaners -- the lacquer thinner works best. (Others have recommended scraping it off with a glass scraper, which I haven't tried.) As when applying the product, wear a protective mask and goggles and also dishwashing gloves to protect your hands.All in all, a very good (and cheap) solution to the privacy problem. I'm surprised this stuff isn't more popular!

I liked the unit a lot when I unwrapped it and immediately topped off two low tires. It worked fine. I was ready for it to be jiggly, noisy, and to take a while from reading other reviews (and because the thing only costs 25 bucks), so none of that bothered me. The inflator tip was quite hard to pull off the valve stem after inflating the tire (and once led to 3-5 lbs of PSI loss), but I think it was particularly tight because it was new.What DID bother me happened last week when I was topping off tires again (I either have 3 slow leaks or rapid, frigid temperature fluctuations have adverse effects on my tires/rims). I topped off two tires again and was checking a third and saw it could it use a few pounds of pressure (the unit works quite well as a simple gauge). So, I pressed the switch to ON...and nothing happened. I had _just_ finished topping off another tire and it had worked fine, and now nada.So, I checked the cigarette lighter socket in the car -- it still had power. And the light on the unit still lit up (a pretty good sign the unit was still getting power). I re-set the inflator tip to go further onto the valve stem and even put it back on the tire it had just worked for and upped the sauto-hutoff setting. Still nothing. Then I went and plugged the unit into another AC/DC power source I have in the house to make sure it wasn't just something crazy with the power draw/socket in my car. Still nothing, but the light would turn on. Took out the fuse from the plug and it looked fine. Tested the fuse with my multimeter and it showed continuity. Tried it one more time from the car, and still got nothing from the compressor motor.As best as I can figure it, the unit still gets power but the compressor won't turn on. Whether this is a malfunction in the motor, the switch, or the auto-shutoff, I have no idea (the auto-shutoff was turned up to be 20 PSI above the PSI of the tire, and still no go). Doesn't really matter. For a device that is meant to be carried in the car to help out in case of emergency, this is pretty much unacceptable. Was the unit simply a lemon? Probably. But you can find cheap inflators like this for around half the price (10-15 bucks), so this wasn't even the cheapest option out there. That means I expect the proportion of lemons to be that much smaller. It still gets two stars because I like the ergonomics of the unit, the light, and the auto-shutoff. And that all worked...until it didn't. After owning the unit for only three weeks and only inflating four tires.Thank goodness for easy return policies. I got my money back on this one, no point in trying another one of these. Instead, I went to the local farm/automotive store and found a two-gallon air compressor (with full accessory set as far as tire chuck, etc.) for 60 bucks. It's not something I can use from the cigarette lighter, but it is far more robust and obviously much faster at inflating tires (without needing to spend a buck at a gas station every time I need a top-off). Sixty bucks isn't bad at all, and I wish I had further researched the air compressor route before buying a 12V inflator. If you really need a portable 12V unit to have in the car with you, something like this unit is nice (as long as it doesn't break), but if you simply want a way to blow up your tires fast and easy at home, I'd recommend a 1 or 2 gallon air compressor that comes with various inflation accessories./chucks. If you DO go the 12V inflator route and absolutely have to have something in the car with you that works, I'd find something cheaper and buy two of them.

This winter has been one long snowpocalypse here in Indiana and that can also bring power outages. This is a must have for anyone who can lose power and experience low enough temperatures to make life either very uncomfortable or put your life in danger.Now this doesn't pertain to Mr. Heater....but I got caught driving in my first major snow squall this year.  If you don't know what a snow squall is (and I didn't either until it hit), you get hit by blinding snow so that you can see ABSOLUTELY NOTHING for a long period of time.  When I say see nothing.....I mean see NOTHING.  This lasted 30 minutes as I sat somewhere on a major highway wondering if I was going to get in a pileup because someone might try to move forward.  I was so blinded by the snow I got disoriented and didn't even know which direction I was facing on the highway.Moral of this little story....be prepared.  I have supplies in my car for lots of emergencies.  Mr. Heater is the item to have at home for such an emergency.

RevText: I bought this knife mainly because Paul Sellers recommended it. It's exactly the one that he uses. He's a rather famous woodworker who's into teaching after a 40-year career as a furniture maker. Stanley sells a plastic-handle version in the US for less and I suspect that it would work as well.The blade on this knife (like that of the other one that I just mentioned) folds into the handle, but in folding it in you have to guide it in. Otherwise the edge of the blade will catch on the edge of the slot in the handle.It comes with 2 blades stored in the handle, so you take the handle apart to load a blade. In so doing I found that the plastic mechanism inside looks fairly flimsy. And while the black plastic piece on the back of the handle seats fully when the blade is fully extended, it does not seat fully when the blade is retracted.So I took it apart again and tried to figure out if I had positioned the plastic parts inside badly when I installed the blade. But I could find nothing wrong. Perhaps it's designed that way.Among the nice things about this knife are the blade shape and the handle shape. The latter is ergonomically well shaped as far as I can tell, and the blade shape and extension permits sharpening without removing the blade, and even the use of the knife in chip carving. This was demonstrated for me by Mr. Sellers in two of his online videos. I think that he mentioned that he has had about three sets of blades in 10 years (something like that). He sharpens the knife every day that he uses it, using coarse, fine and extra-fine diamond "stones", and as he demonstrated that it took him perhaps 15 seconds to touch up the edge--- 5 seconds per stone.Furthermore, the little screw in the back end does not go into a tapped hole in the cast aluminum-alloy handle (aluminium to you British) but instead goes into a tapped hole in a steel insert--- a quality feature.So on the whole I like this knife. I'm using it to scribe wood that I'm cutting one way or another and of course I'm getting sharp cuts. I'm also not having trouble with the blade tracking the straight edge. But I just wish that the plastic innards were not what they are but were of more durable material and less sloppy.I paid only about $12 with shipping for mine, from Amazon, through a British seller. That other Stanley knife is the "Stanley 10-049 Pocket Knife with Rotating Blade" and replacement blades for it are sold on Amazon as the "Stanley 11-041 Utility Replacement Blade". Those blades have a shape that is different from those of the knife that I'm reviewing.

RevText: I usually use a router to make dado cuts, but there are some uses like lap joints that are better to do with a dado head.  The Freud 508 set is less expensive than Forrest's Dado King, but it got a good review in Fine Woodworking, so I ordered it.  It's been several years since I've used a dado set, and now I remember why -- setting up is a bit of a pain.  But...  I tried making lap joints once on a router and had to interrupt the work with a trip the emergency room for a few stitches.  To get reacquainted with dado sets, I made some 3/4" wide x 1/4" deep cuts with the Freud set in some scrap walnut, in melamine-clad particle board and in cherry plywood. The cuts  were perfectly smooth, with a perfectly flat profile and no tear-out at the exit.  Very impressive that it can handle such different materials.The set comes in a plastic case with very thin plastic spacers to separate the chippers and blades.  I don't think these will hold up very well, but it will be easy enough to make substitutes.  There's a useful DVD behind the foam in the upper section of the case, along with a chart showing how to combine the blades and chippers for various widths.This is one of several Freud dado sets.  Less expensive sets than this one use chippers that use two pairs of cutters rather than four, and that may result in less smooth cuts.  The next step up (SD608) uses a device that offers an additional width -- 7/32" -- and uses an adjustable insert to eliminate the need for shims and reduce the amount of shuffling of chippers and that you need to do to change widths.  But unless you need to change widths frequently during each session, this set (SD508) is an excellent choice.  It will definitely give you a good range of widths and clean, accurate cuts.

This 20% Salicylic Acid works through layers of skin to start killing the acne infection right away and often keeps it from ever coming to the surface.At first sign of acne I use this great roll-on applicator to dab a bit on that spot and leave it (no rinse). I will continue to use this as an occasional all-over facial, but much more so as an acne spot treatment.This has become a staple in my medicine cabinet and my most powerful tool for managing my acne.

AMBRE SULTAN is like Prince Husain's journey in "One Thousand and One Nights". This deliciously orange syrup is made of coriander, amber, oregano, bay leaf, myrtle, angelica root, sandalwood, patchouli, benzoin, and vanilla. From the first spritz you are transported to far off lands. The fragrance is strong and starts off with heavy almost medicinal herbs, which give way to the glorious and rich amber tempered by sandalwood and vanilla. The dry-down is amazing - reminds me of creme brulee. Unlike traditional amber fragrances, this is not powdery and light but rich and unctuous with great longevity and sillage all tempered by the masterful blending of ingredients. The benzoin and resins are quit prominent like incense burning in a mosque, which adds to the mystery. Serge Lutens and Christopher Seldrake (the "nose" behind this remarkable fragrance) are geniuses. I find that less is more with this fragrance, which is a monster and will last all day. Too much and it is offensive as this fragrance unfolds quickly and mysteriously like revealing the genie after rubbing a magic lamp. I later called Liddell customer service and inquired about that and they said it is straight up alcohol, and if you don't want to be consuming alcohol you're best to stop taking it. So, that was interesting and might possibly help others to know. One question that made me ask is, "Can this product make you fail an alcohol test?" I don't know, but no one seems to be able to definitely answer that, and that is a red flag to me.I honestly don't really know what exactly to think of the product. I would like to speak about the comparison between Mont Blanc Individuel and Original Santal. I am a huge fan of Original Santal. It's just a wonderful fragrance. I like Mont Blanc Individuel as well! However, these are two separate fragrances, and I would not recommend Mont Blanc Individuel as a "replacement" for Original Santal at all. Likewise, Mont Blanc Individuel also serves its purpose.The opening of Mont Blanc Individuel smells exactly like Original Santal after Original Santal has dried down for about 3 minutes. There's no doubt about it. Sure, the Creed smells more fresh and natural, but unless you are VERY familiar with Original Santal, you would not be able to tell the difference. This smell stays similar to Original Santal for about an hour. Then things start to change.Mont Blanc Individuel changes drastically from smelling like Original Santal to smelling like laundry fresh out of the dryer. Is that bad? Absolutely not! But Original Santal has an intoxicating smell that has more to it than the "dryer sheet" smell. Individuel, after about an hour, is pure dryer sheets. Original Santal has more spice. I would even say that after three hours of wearing Mont Blanc Individuel, you can't even compare the two fragrances. If I didn't smell Individuel's opening, I wouldn't have even thought the two fragrances were even remotely similar.I'm not just repeating other people's comparisons of dryer sheets -- no, this really smells like dryer sheets! Like I said, that's not a bad thing. This is an excellent, fresh smelling fragrance. The best part of fragrance is in its first hour.I would also say that Mont Blanc Individuel is more masculine and Original Santal is more unisex. I would love to smell Original Santal on a woman. Unfortunately, my girlfriend doesn't like to wear it.Don't go believing all these people who say a certain fragrance smells exactly like another. They don't. They may share some similarities, but the DNA is totally different from fragrance to fragrance.My advice to anyone considering one of these two fragrances is this: If you are looking for a blind buy, and price is not an issue, go with Original Santal. If you have the opportunity to test Mont Blanc Individuel, go for it. If you find you love the opening a lot more than the drydown, go with Original Santal. The entire drydown of Original Santal is the opening of Mont Blanc Individuel. If you are strapped for cash and just want to smell good, go with Individuel. If you have Original Santal, I do recommend buying Mont Blanc Individuel, because it is a different fragrance, contrary to what others will tell you.Mont Blanc Individuel is a great fragrance on its own. It does not replace Original Santal by any means, but the two fragrances are different. Original Santal is a masterpiece for Creed. Mont Blanc Individuel is very close to being a designer masterpiece on its own. The longevity is outstanding. It projects well without being offensive. And to top it all off, it just smells fresh!Longevity: 10+ hoursProjection: About 3 feetSmell: 7/10Overall: 8/10Mont Blanc Individuel is a great value, is highly versatile and can be worn at any time of the year. I highly recommend adding this fragrance to your collection.----Side Note----I purchased this product directly from Amazon and I can confirm I received an authentic, quality product. Buy with confidence.
RevTitle: Great Fragrance, However, Not a Replacement For Original Santal

Six years ago, if anyone would have told me that I'd soon become passionate about a line of soaps and cleaners, I'd have laughed them right out of my shop. I've never been one to worry about coming into contact with chemicals. Back in the old days a lot of backyard mechanics like myself used to wash greasy parts and our hands in gasoline, diesel, turpentine, kerosene etc. (hey it worked great and was cheap). I know guys who still do this.My wife and I had heard about Cal Ben Five Star Soap on a late night satellite radio show, and after the wife was diagnosed with Stage 3C Ovarian Cancer and began chemotherapy, we really began to make an effort at eliminating chemicals from our lives as much as we practicably could. One of the things we did was to order a sample pack of Cal Ben's more popular products.We both agreed after our first shower with the bar soap and shampoo that we could not only feel the difference on our skin, but for whatever reason, "felt" better mentally. It was just a change in mood, so it's hard to explain, but getting out of the shower and toweling off after the first shower with Cal Ben, I just had a clean and more positive feeling. I felt more alert and in a more positive mood than normal. I didn't expect or even want the stuff to be any different from my Dial soap, because ordering bar soap on-line seemed like it would be a hassle. I couldn't deny that the soap got my skin as clean as any other soap I've used (if not cleaner) and did it with all natural ingredients. We immediately placed an order for a four year bundled supply of all the Cal Ben 5 Star Soap products. Though not available on Amazon or through this seller that I know of, I'd like to add that we also really love the liquid dish soap (best we've ever used) and the powdered laundry soap.Those with sensitive skin might be interested in my mother's experience with the Cal Ben line. Mom has a rare auto immune disease on top of allergies to just about any and all soaps,cleaners and perfumes. She's never been able to find a laundry detergent that didn't cause her some pain and rash, and could never even think about using a laundry powder. Most bar soaps and many shampoos would cause her to develop an itchy red rash as well. I tried for three years to get her to try Cal Ben. Last year she finally agreed to let us give her some of the laundry powder, bar soap, shampoo and dish soap. She was reluctant to try anything new to her, so she started off with the dish soap, and when she found that it made her hands feel great, she ventured on to the bar soap, shampoo and finally the dreaded laundry powder. A week later, she called and wanted to know if we could sell her some of our personal supply. Even though Mom liked the Cal Ben laundry soap, she has opted to buy Cal Ben's liquid laundry detergent simply because of her bad experiences with other laundry powders, but has had to reluctantly admit that all these products have changed her life (she hates it when I'm right). We ended up placing a big order with Cal Ben and dividing the product between us.Amazon prices fluctuate wildly at times so I will leave that matter up to the shopper to decide. I'm reviewing the product, not this particular seller, which on Amazon can change abruptly. We order directly from Cal Ben and spend $450 (including shipping) on the "Super Star `4800' Collection" package that includes a four year supply of bar soap, dish soap, laundry detergent and shampoo. Cleaning products are very heavy, so ordering in bulk really cuts down on shipping costs per unit and makes it convenient to not have to keep a close eye on our supply. This is the most economical and convenient route for us, but for those who aren't looking to lay out that much money at one time on cleaning products or who don't have room to store a half pallet of supplies, then buying a little at a time and paying more per unit may very well be your best option.However you do it, DO give this bar soap and all the Cal-ben Five Star Soap line a chance. I believe you'll find, like our family, that you love the product line and will feel good about buying a product that is made here in the good ol' US of A.

I apply it twice a day, though the instructions say you can apply it up to three times a day.  I also wear sunscreen every day which helps also.  In addition, the instructions say to avoid the sun. I was surprised at first to see the toothpicks.  You are supposed to twist a little cotton (not included) around each toothpick to make your own applicators.  Do they really expect us to make our own Q-tips?  How could I twist the cotton on?  How could I make sure it wouldn't fall off when I was using it?  I read that other reviewers used disposable mascara wands so I bought them.When I used the kit yesterday, I was surprised to find that it was really easy to twist a bit of cotton on the toothpicks and it didn't fall off!  In fact, for tinting my brows, I decided that I liked using the cotton toothpicks better than the mascara wands.The first time I did my brows, I used the same applicator on both brows per solution.  One brow came out darker than the other!  (The brow I used the applicator on first must have got more solution than the second.)  So I redid the second brow which then looked slightly fuller than the first, but I decided it would have to be good enough.  I learned from this experience to use a fresh applicator of solution for each brow.My eyebrows came out really dark, but my eyelashes hardly absorbed any color at all.  I wondered if the petroleum jelly that was recommended to surround the eyes might have got on my lashes or if I had not washed my lashes well enough.  I tried tinting my eyelashes again today.  I carefully washed them and used no petroleum jelly on the surrounding skin.  It did not work any better the second time!  I used plenty of solution on the mascara wands.  (Could my habitual use of mascara affect my lashes so that they are less susceptible to coloring?)Another thing I learned was to leave the three little bottles in the box at all times!  When I was trying everything out for the first time I got out the three bottles and while I had the first one open I reached for something and accidentally knocked it over!  (Oh, no!)  The box has slots for holding the bottles which would have kept this accident from happening.There are two solution bottles (#1 and #2).  The 3rd bottle is for erasing mistakes.  You put solution #1 on first and let it dry.  Then put on solution #2.  You will immediately see your brows (and maybe lashes) start to darken.The paper insert said that lighter shades could be achieved by mixing drops of solution with drops of water in a glass dish.P.S.  I recommend that you try this on a day when you don't have to go anywhere, since it can stain the skin under your brows and look a little strange at first -- like a messy job with an eyebrow pencil.  Fortunately, the skin staining will wear off over the next few days.  On the 2nd day, my brows look a little better.  On the 3rd day, I actually like how they look.

RevText: OVERALL REVIEW:Speaking as a product junkie who prides herself on knowing a good product and being objective, I have to say this is an awesome product.  Yes, it's a bit pricey but the benefits are well worth it. My skin is brighter, smoother and softer. Reduced acne and large pores..............Want or need to know more?  Keep reading :) ...........MY SKIN:I am in my early 40's and have mocha brown skin which tends to get oily in certain areas of my face.  I also suffer from adult acne which can range from a pimple or 2 or 10! These of course, leave some acne scars (due to extraction) but once I have that under control with the use of creams, treatments and use of peels....life is ok!  This past year I began seeing large pores around my cheek area and noticed my face had become uneven in skin tone.  Yikes! *faint*MY(old) REGIMEN:I used at home  salicylic and glycolic (liquid kind) peels every other week.  Exfoliated in between peels and was diligent about keeping my skin and pores clean. However, using these peels I had to wait a week before seeing results and sometimes afraid I would burn my skin, leave on too long or just make my situation worse.  I had anxiety each time I used them, so I was extra careful and received good results.  One day when I went to re-order my peels  I stumbled across "Instant Peel".  I figured, what the heck and here we are.HOW I USED THE PRODUCT:The product recommends that you use it in the shower, which I have found is the best method (yeah I tried other non-shower methods like steaming face, warm damp towel on face, etc). There are 6 packets and it is creamy in texture (not thick-creamy a bit liquidy).1. Once in the shower for about 1-2 minutes (your face has to be moist/damp NOT wet), squeeze out a little bit onto the tips  of your fingers.  With your fingers, smooth liquidy cream onto an area of your face; then, using back and forth motion apply light to moderate pressure (don't massage it in using a circular motion-go back and forth). The dead skin will roll off onto your fingers. Just rinse your fingers pat dry with a cloth (hang one over the shower rod where you can get to it easily). I found that doing one side of my face (a cheek and jawline) at the same time works best. I use about 33-40% of the product for each side of my face (twice).  Doing smaller sections works well too but if you have a lot of dead skin then you will spend a little more time in the shower and possibly risk running out of hot water!  :)  Rinse off the product from fingers and splash a little on face to get rid of the residue.2. Repeat process on other side and forehead. I liken this peeling process to having Elmers Glue (white stuff we used in school during art time) being semi-dry on your hands and you roll it off to be free of gluey hands.  You will know when all of the dead skin is off your face because you will not be able to roll anymore off.3. BEWARE!  If you rub too hard and continue to rub vigorously past the "no more rolling required" point you will cause your face to be raw and red and even perhaps end up damaging your skin (yes, this is what happened to me! I was overly excited).  Just be sure to stop rubbing when the skin stops rolling off onto your fingers and you'll be fine. The product isn't supposed to affect new skin cells but, again, if you rub like a mad woman (i.e., yours truly) then there is a risk of hurting your skin.  So just don't do it!  :)SIDE NOTE & TIP:Unbeknownst to me, when I first used the product I had so much dead skin on my face it was unreal!  I was sure I would have very little dead skin cell removal because I exfoliated regularly.  Ha!  wrong.  I ended up using a pack and a half of product.  If you have product left over put the unused portion/packet in a ziplock bag and save for next time. Make sure to seal it. This is important because the product will dry out and go bye-bye.THE RESULTS:Once done showering, I dried off, patted face dry and couldn't believe my eyes when I looked in the mirror.  My skin was literally and noticeably brighter and more even toned. After one use?? The large pores on my cheeks had reduced in size, acne pimples drastically reduced in size, face looked younger (a solid 5 years-Girl Scouts' Honor!!), skin was radiant looking and felt baby soft smooth. Again, this was after the first use! I stood in literal awe. Amazing!!!!!  I have not used my at home liquid peels since then.  I continued using this product because this one does the trick and you see instant results.  My make-up goes on smoother and people comment on my skin and it's texture. That's a whole new thing for me.  When I first started using the product I used it 2 times the first week (3 packets) and then once every other week (1 packet). The entire box lasted about 2-1/2 months.  I am now on box #2.  The benefits are so great that this is now a part of my (new) face care regimen. So glad I invested in this product and stumbled across the page.  I love the way my skin looks and feels. I haven't seen my skin this "bright and glowy" in yearsIn case you are wondering......MY(new)REGIMEN:Use peel once every two weeks (only have to use 1 packet now).  After using the peel,  I use a quality oil control astringent, and a light moisturizer. In between peels, I use a glycolic exfoliating wash every 2-3 days and this along with the Instant Peels have helped keep the dreaded acne at bay. I will also note that I have not had as much dead skin removal since the first time I used it.  My skin continues to look youthful and the acne marks/spots are lighter. My skin tone has evened out quite a bit especially near the jawline.  I love this stuff!  It really is amazing!  Yayyy :)

I have had a small wart on my chest for most of my life.  I have applied the wart medicine  Compound W Fast Acting Gel on the wart for about three days (once in the morning and once in the evening) and covered it with three small pieces of automotive tape to cover only the wart and to deprive it from its oxygen supply.  So far half of the wart has been removed with the medicine and tape.  It is important to get the wart nice and soft before you apply the medicine on it so soak it down for about ten minutes in the morning and ten minutes in the evening then pat it dry.  After that, apply the medicine and tape over the wart.  I have used a QTip to apply the wart medicine,  a scissor to cut the automotive tape and a tweezer to clean the scab from on top and around the wart each time to allow the medicine to properly sink in.  Those with much larger warts may have to use this product for a longer period of time to see its effect but this product does work and if applied in the right way, you should be able to see results faster.  If my wart was bigger I would apply it three times per day.

This is just my experience that I wanted to share, everyone is different (especially when it comes to skin). All you can really do is try it for yourself :)I was so excited to try this cleansing oil, I'd heard a lot of great things about it. Being a huge proponent for organic and natural living, I love the idea of not cleaning my skin with bubbles, namely sodium laurel sulfates and petroleum derived petrochemicals, fragrances, and parabens. The idea of washing my face the way Cleopatra and the ancient Egyptians did appealed to me. Slathering oil onto my face just felt right, like this is how washing your face is supposed to feel.I gave this cleansing oil 2.5 weeks, then couldn't take it anymore. I followed the directions completely, rubbing it onto dry skin and rinsing thoroughly. I loved the way it felt on my face, and I could feel the debris it was pulling out of my pores. By the end of the facial cleanse, it was like the oil had turned into an exfoliating scrub because it had pulled out so much gunk that the oil turned grainy. It was like all that nastiness you see on a Biore strip after you peel it from your nose but in your hands from rubbing the oil. It was amazing and made my skin feel so clean and soft. But then, after a few days of using the oil, I developed the largest, most painful cystic acne breakout I've ever experienced. I have oily skin with slight to moderate hormonal acne, but had never experienced a breakout quite like this.I didn't give up on the oil right away, instead I thought of what could be causing it. Surely, it can't be the oil clogging my pores and causing the breakouts because it's all rinsed away cleanly, right? So I thought maybe because its deep cleaning my pores so well, the grime and bacteria from my makeup brushes (foundation, powder, concealer, blush, blenders, eye brushes, brow brushes, etc.) were getting in and causing the horrific breakout. I cleaned all my brushes very thoroughly and kept on top of cleaning them every week, but this didn't make the cystic acne stop. After dealing with the pain and unsightly acne for 2.5 weeks with no relief in sight, I gave up on the oil. The breakouts subsided and I'm just now getting back to my pre-oil skin (it's been almost 2 months since I stopped). I have a few large, dark acne scars around my chin that are still there and will take a few more months to completely heal and fade away. The breakouts were pretty much all over face: my chin, a bit on my cheeks, along each side of my nose, all over my upper lip and a few on my forehead. It was the worst, most concentrated around my chin and upper lip, however.I gave it two stars because it really does deep clean and made my skin feel great after using it (especially compared to regular facial cleansers) minus the cysts of course. I have about 2/3 of the bottle left, and maybe if I learn something new about why I broke out so badly I'll try it again someday.

I have used this product for about 4 years now and I absolutely love it! I am a natural blonde but with age (as we all probably know) my naturally bleach blonde hair turned into more of a golden/dirty blonde :( and I did not want that. Since my mom refused to let me dye my hair, I did my research and found this miracle of a product.It REALLY WORKS! At some point in those past 4 years I got my hair to very very very light (almost looked like it was dyed) blonde that was a beautiful color with streaks of lighter and darker highlights. And that is my favorite part about this product. If you look up close to the the hair (after you've been using it for a while) you will see that there is at least 10 different shades of blonde in that little bunch of hair. It doesn't look tacky as it may seem from my description but rather it looks very beautiful and natural (just like the sun did it ;) ).I stopped using it for a year because I decided I wanted darker hair and I mean it did look like growing out hair for a while but that's because I was lazy and didn't apply it correctly.THE BEST WAY TO USE IT:Make sure your hair is damp but not too wet because you're about to blowdry it until it's dry. Brush your hair out so it's not tangled, apply some heat protectant for all the heat you're about to use on your hair and comb it through again. If you are serious about lightening your hair, I suggest you do it in layers. Section of horizontal layers from bottom to top of your hair and follow this procedure. Spray the product everywhere you'd like to see your hair lightened (I also like to take off the orange flap thing because I just find it annoying while spraying). Make sure to BRUSH YOUR HAIR THROUGH once all the product you want in that layer is in! This is very important because if you don't do this you might end up with a solid line of roots once your hair starts to grow out and it won't look as natural because the color is concentrated in one place. Go through the stands with a blowdryer on hot and high (it burns so take breaks if you need to). Once that layer is dry, move on to the next level until you reach top of your head. By now your hair should be fully dry. If you want you can also straighten your hair after this for the added effect concentrating the heat on the sprayed areas but just be aware of how much heat you're putting on your hair all at once (and don't complain later that it's drying out your hair).If you would like to have more concentrations in certain areas of your head (such as face framing) then you should take a cotton ball, spray the product on it and then run the cotton ball down the strands you want most product on. I did this for the hair line around my face and it looked amazing!!I also did only the top half of my hair so that the bottom is still natural and darker than the top layer because I like it and I'm too lazy to go through every hair on my head :PLastly, the bad things:-Just like any hair coloring product, you have to keep up with the roots if they do grow out because this lightness isn't fading away anywhere (FYI)!-It's challenging to color all of your hair because it's just so much effort. Ask a friend if you have to to make sure you cover all the hair you want lightened with the product. When I went crazy with making my top layers super light, I didn't like how the layers under that were peeking through and were significantly darker than the top :/ Also, don't forget to color the hair when you were to put it in a ponytail but that's just my personal preference.Overall, this is a WONDERFUL product and I am so glad I found it and I do not look like a box blonde. It's looks natural and beautiful and it's super easy and CHEAP! :)

Using this mask with just water or apple cider vinegar will definitely give you noticeably smoother skin for a short while but I didn't find it anything spectacular.  Not one to needlessly waste anything I've purchased I decided to figure out some ways to improve this mask.  I used up a whole tub of this clay trying many different ingredients and have come up with a few I am really fond of.LIQUIDAPPLE CIDER VINEGAR- The traditional way to use this mask.  Others have extolled it virtues so I won't go into detail here, but it is a universally great choice for many skin types.  ACV makes the smoothest and easiest to apply mixture as well.ROSE WATER - This is currently my preferred way to use this mask.  Rosewater makes your face beautifully soft and it smells divine.  Even better, rose water is anti-inflammatory and full of antioxidants.  It is also balancing to both dry and oily skin.  If you can't find plain rosewater a rosewater and glycerin toner can be used just as well.WITCH HAZEL - I use witch hazel when I'm battling breakouts.  It's a mild astringent that doesn't dry out your skin like many other astringents have a tendency to do.ESSENTIAL OILS - I use 2 drops of each oil and generally use 1-2 oils per mask.TEA TREE - Perfect for those looking to use this mask as a way to control acne.  A couple of drops of tea tree oil quickly stop pimples from getting any larger and helps dry them out in 1/3 of the time it usually takes.NEEM - Neem oil is known to be anti-viral, anti-bacterial, and anti-inflammatory among other properties.  It is wonderful for those with acne-prone skin, dry skin and conditions like eczema.CHAMOMILE - This oil is anti-inflammatory and will help to reduce redness in your face.  I use this when my skin is chapped from harsh winter weather.LAVENDER - Soothing and softening, lavender is not just good for your skin, but a couple of drops will also mask the overwhelming scents of apple cider vinegar, tea tree and/or neem oils.OTHER ADDITIONSActivated Charcoal - Activated charcoal takes the purifying qualities of this mask and bumps it up a few dozen notches.  Activated charcoal makes for an incredible mask on its own, but is quite messy and can be difficult to remove from your skin.  A better way to benefit from its properties is to take a a capsule, break it open and add 1/2 to 1 capsule of charcoal into the mask.  Just search for 'activated charcoal capsule' if you aren't familiar with the product.Oatmeal  - Oatmeal is well-known for its moisturizing properties so if you have dry skin adding some oatmeal flour is a helpful addition.  You can take plain (NOT flavored/sugared pouches) oatmeal and run it through your food processor until pretty fine.  It doesn't need to be perfectly evenly ground.  You can also add the oat flour you find in bags in the flour aisle of the grocery store.Honey - Excellent for moisturizing your skin as well as treating acne as honey is antibacterial.  Honey is also full of antioxidants which are beneficial to your skin. Honey is also anti-inflammatory.  Don't be scared, it rinses off cleanly with just warm water and leaves no sticky residue.  Use raw honey for the best results.I hope this has helped you some!
